You have two options in the FastAPI docs: **Server-Sent Events (SSE)** for one-way server-to-browser streaming, or **WebSockets** for a two-way connection.

### Option 1: Server-Sent Events

SSE is a standard for streaming data from the server to the client over HTTP.[2] SSE is commonly used for AI chat streaming, live notifications, logs and observability, and other cases where the server pushes updates to the client.[2] It uses the `text/event-stream` format, which is supported natively by browsers with the `EventSource` API[2]. SSE support was added in FastAPI 0.135.0.[2]

The excerpt I found doesn't include the endpoint code. You can find it on the full SSE page: https://fastapi.tiangolo.com/tutorial/server-sent-events/

### Option 2: WebSockets

First, add `websockets` (a Python library that makes it easy to use the "WebSocket" protocol) to your project[1]. In your WebSocket route you can `await` for messages and send messages.[4]

```python
from fastapi import FastAPI, WebSocket

app = FastAPI()

@app.websocket("/ws")
async def websocket_endpoint(websocket: WebSocket):
    await websocket.accept()
    while True:
        data = await websocket.receive_text()
        await websocket.send_text(f"Message text was: {data}")
```

In the browser, the docs' example connects with JavaScript: `var ws = new WebSocket("ws://localhost:8000/ws");` and handles incoming messages in `ws.onmessage`. You can receive and send binary, text, and JSON data.[4] Full guide: https://fastapi.tiangolo.com/advanced/websockets/

If you broadcast to many clients from an in-memory list, it will only work while the process is running, and will only work with a single process.[3] For something more robust, the docs point to encode/broadcaster[3].
